rules.banned_because: Someone else's names, kept out of everything Euphonia publishes (Appendix E; setting/ip-review.md).
rules.fey_type_because: "Fey" survives only as the creature type; the setting's prose says "fae" (Book Two, What's Different). The 2024 rules' own names keep it too: Fey Ancestry, Fey Touched, Fey Wanderer, Summon Fey and the SRD's Conjure Fey (Chat, 15 November). So does a list of creature types: "any Undead, Fey, or Elemental".
rules.renames_because: The setting's own names for those planes, the first two of the Revelator's Cosmography: the Feywild is the Hidden, the Shadowfell the Ghostlands (setting/whats-out.md, wheel-and-plenum.md). The SRD's "the Feywild" reads "the Hidden".

data.name: Counsellor
data.blurb: Int. The people class: spymasters, marshals, factors, majordomos, gamesters, and the Hollowed.

traits.value: *Choose 3:* Deception, History, Insight, Investigation, Medicine, Nature, Perception, Sleight of Hand, Stealth, or Survival
Simple weapons, and Martial weapons that have the Finesse or Light property
*Choose 1:* Forgery Kit, Cartographer's Tools, Gaming Set (one of your choice), or Poisoner's Kit
*Choose A or B:* (A) Rapier, Light Crossbow, 20 Bolts, Crossbow Bolt Case, Dagger, Scholar's Pack, the tool you chose, and 2 GP; or (B) 110 GP.

rows.Class Features: Ability Score Improvement, Read About It

features.name: Calculation
features.text:
**Defense.** You are where the blow isn't. While you aren't wearing armor or wielding a Shield, your base Armor Class equals 10 plus your Dexterity and Intelligence modifiers. If another feature gives you a way to calculate your Armor Class without armor, choose one. You can't add your Intelligence modifier to your Armor Class more than once.

**Strike.** You hit where the numbers say. When you make an attack roll with a Simple weapon, or with a Martial weapon that has the Finesse or Light property, you can use your Intelligence modifier instead of your Strength or Dexterity modifier for the attack and damage rolls.

features.name: Encyclopedic
features.text: You have read everything. You gain proficiency in two of the following skills of your choice: Arcana, History, Nature, or Religion. If you already have proficiency in a skill you choose, choose another from the same list.

features.name: Observe
features.text:
You build a model of every fight, and every room, from what you see in it. As a Bonus Action, choose a creature you can see within 60 feet of yourself. The creature becomes **Observed** by you for 1 minute, and you learn one of the following facts about it of your choice:

- Which of its ability scores is highest.
- Which of its saving throws has the lowest bonus.
- One damage Resistance, Immunity, or Vulnerability it has (the DM chooses if it has several, and tells you if it has none).
- Whether it is Bloodied.
- Whether it is hurt, sick, exhausted, drunk, or poisoned.
- Its trade or station, as its hands, dress, and bearing show it.
- Whether it is armed or carrying something concealed, and roughly what.

When you Observe a creature within 10 feet of you, you learn one more fact about it.

You can Observe a creature that is already Observed, to learn another fact and start the minute again. Any number of creatures can be Observed by you at once. Wherever this class says "Observed," it means Observed by you. While you have the Incapacitated condition, you can't use any feature that works only against an Observed creature.

You learn only what can be seen, heard, or measured. Observe never tells you what a creature thinks, feels, or intends.

features.name: Exploit
features.text:
When a creature you can see hits an Observed creature you can see with an attack roll, you can point out the weakness (no action required). You decide after the attack hits and before its damage is rolled. The attack deals the extra damage shown in the Exploit column of the Counsellor Features table. These dice aren't rolled twice on a Critical Hit. The extra damage is the same type as the attack's damage; if the attack deals more than one type, you choose one of them. The attacker can be you, an ally, or any other creature.

You can't use Exploit before your first turn in a combat, and once you use it, you can't use it again until the start of your next turn.

features.name: Sidestep
features.text:
You saw it coming and were already moving. When a creature you can see hits you with an attack roll, you can take a Reaction to halve the attack's damage against you (round down). You can then move up to 10 feet without provoking Opportunity Attacks.

You can use Sidestep and Anticipate (level 2) a combined number of times equal to your Counsellor level (minimum of two), and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Short or Long Rest. From level 5, they have no limit on uses (see Wider Gaze). A multiclass Counsellor uses one pool instead (As a Multiclass Character).

features.name: Direct
features.text:
Once per turn when you Observe a creature on your turn, you can also choose one ally within 60 feet of yourself who can see or hear you. The next time the ally makes an attack roll or an ability check against an Observed creature before the start of your next turn (to hit it, to talk it round, to read it, or to fool it), it can roll your **computation die** and add the number rolled. The ally decides after seeing the d20 roll but before knowing whether it succeeds.

The Computation Die column of the Counsellor Features table shows the size of your computation die: a d4 at level 2 and a d8 from level 5.

features.name: Anticipate
features.text:
When an Observed creature you can see hits you or a creature within 30 feet of you with an attack roll, you can take a Reaction to roll your computation die and subtract the number rolled from the attack roll, possibly turning the hit into a miss. Anticipate shares its uses with Sidestep.

When the hit is on you, you choose: Sidestep for the sure half and a step out of reach, or Anticipate to try to erase it. When it's on an ally, Anticipate is the one you have.

features.name: Deduction
features.text:
You can go quiet and compute. You can spend 10 minutes in stillness, doing nothing but thinking, and then ask the DM one question about a creature, an object, a place, or an event that you have Observed or seen, or whose evidence you have examined. The DM answers with the most likely truth that follows from what you have observed, in a sentence or two. If what you have observed isn't enough to support an answer, the DM tells you so, and the use isn't expended.

The answer is about what is and what is likely to happen: where the smuggler took the cargo, which of three doors is trapped, how many guards will be on the wall at midnight. It never tells you what a creature thinks or feels. If anything you based the answer on was false (a forged letter, a disguise, a lie you believed), the answer follows from the false data, and the DM doesn't tell you so.

The answer moves the case forward without closing it: where to look, who to ask, what doesn't fit. A question that would end a mystery gets the piece of it the evidence supports. The DM can hold an answer until the end of the scene or your next rest; the use isn't expended until the answer is given.

Deduction isn't an ability check, and there's nothing to roll: an Intelligence (Investigation) check finds the clues, and Deduction is what you conclude from them. You can use Deduction a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of once), and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Mental Index
features.text: Choose two of your skill proficiencies. You have Expertise with those skills.

features.name: Counsellor Discipline
features.text: You gain a Counsellor subclass of your choice: the Factor, the Gamester, the Hollowed, the Majordomo, the Marshal, or the Spymaster. A subclass is a specialization that grants you features at certain Counsellor levels. For the rest of your career, you gain each of your subclass's features that are of your Counsellor level or lower.

features.name: Ability Score Improvement
features.text: You gain the Ability Score Improvement feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. You gain this feature again at Counsellor levels 8, 12, and 16.

features.name: Read About It
features.text: You may never have done it, but you have read about it. When you make an ability check with a skill or a tool you aren't proficient in, you can add your Proficiency Bonus to the check; decide before you roll. The bonus replaces any other feature that adds part of your Proficiency Bonus to that check, such as Jack of All Trades. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Short or Long Rest.

features.name: Wider Gaze
features.text: You can Observe a creature within 120 feet of yourself, and when you do, you learn two facts about it instead of one (three if it's within 10 feet of you). Sidestep and Anticipate no longer have a limited number of uses.

features.name: Agile Nerves
features.text: When you're subjected to an effect that allows you to make a Dexterity saving throw to take only half damage, you instead take no damage if you succeed on the saving throw and only half damage if you fail. You can't use this feature while you have the Incapacitated condition.

features.name: Outdo
features.text: What you know, you know cold. When you make an ability check with a skill or tool in which you have Expertise, you can treat a d20 roll of 9 or lower as a 10.

features.name: Total Recall
features.text: You forget nothing. You remember everything you have seen, heard, or read in the last year, word for word, and you can recall it at will. The DM can ask you to keep your own notes at the table and treat them as your character's memory: what you wrote down, your character recalls word for word. Deduction now takes 1 minute instead of 10.

features.name: Cold Read
features.text: When you roll Initiative, you can Observe one creature you can see (no action required). Exploit's dice also grow at this level, and again at levels 13 and 17, as the Exploit column of the Counsellor Features table shows.

features.name: Closed Mind
features.text: You gain proficiency in Wisdom saving throws. If you already have it, you instead gain proficiency in Constitution or Charisma saving throws (your choice).

features.name: Never Surprised
features.text: You have Advantage on Initiative rolls, and you can't have Disadvantage on them.

features.name: Far Projection
features.text: Deduction can answer a question about what is likely to happen up to a year from now, not only what is likely soon. The DM answers with the course events will most likely take if no one acts on what you learn, and can give the answer at the start of the next session.

features.name: Unreadable
features.text: Your mind is a closed room. Unless you allow it, magic can't read your thoughts or determine whether you are lying, and divination magic can't perceive you or learn your location (as with *Locate Creature* or *Scrying*). You also have Immunity to the Charmed condition.

features.name: Epic Boon
features.text: You gain an Epic Boon feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. Boon of Truesight is recommended.

features.name: Checkmate
features.text:
You see every piece at once. Your Intelligence score increases by 2, to a maximum of 22. In addition, when you roll Initiative, you Observe every creature you can see (no action required). You learn Observe's facts about only one of them, your choice. The others stay Observed only until the end of the first round of the combat, unless you Observe them again: the opening is yours.

> **Playing a Counsellor**
>
> You don't have to be a genius to play one. The rules do the computing: Observe and Deduction are questions, and the DM answers them the way a trained mind would. Your job is to ask the right question at the right time. "What's it weakest against?" on turn one; "Where did the smuggler take the cargo?" after you've walked the docks.
>
> Say what you see. When you Observe, tell the table what you've learned, then say what it means: "It favors its left side. Hit it there." Exploit only works when someone hits, so the party needs to hear where to aim.
>
> Counsellors in the field are seldom at the back. Sidestep takes half the blow and moves you out of it, and you learn more about anything you're close enough to touch: the one at the Fighter's shoulder sees the tell, calls it, and is gone before the second swing.
>
> Being right is the fun, and being right is also the friction. Direct is advice, and your allies can ignore it. Let them. A Counsellor who's right and gets overruled is a better scene than one who's obeyed. Deduction runs on what you observed: if someone has fed you a lie, you'll be confidently wrong, and you won't know it.
>
> If you play one of the Hollowed, make sure your table has talked about boundaries beforehand. A mind that computes without feeling is a hard fit for a party, and each table works out for itself how hard. Know the pitfalls going in, and keep the coldness in character.

> **Answering a Counsellor (for the DM)**
>
> Deduction and the Disciplines' questions (Staff Officer, Lay of the Land, Siegecraft, The Hum, Follow the Money) ask you for true answers on the spot. A few habits keep that easy.
>
> **Give the next step, not the last.** "Who killed the factor?" in the first scene gets the lead the evidence supports: the ink on the cuff, the clerk who was paid twice, the door that was locked from the wrong side. The player gets a true answer every time, and what you hand over is a scene to play; the story keeps going.
>
> **Take your time.** You can hold an answer until the end of the scene or the next rest, and a Far Projection until the start of the next session; the use isn't spent until you answer. If you haven't decided the thing they're asking about, decide it now, or tell them when they'll know.
>
> **The hints.** A few lines in this class say something is happening to Counsellors: there are more of them than there were, sleep comes harder, the mind closes without being taught to, and a Factor's underwritten claims pay more often than they should. The cause is a kind of mind. Some people reason and reckon faster than anyone should and know things they can't account for, and 1668 has no idea to hold what they are. No test the century has finds magic in them, so the courts hire them as clever servants and fold them into the power structure without knowing what they've taken on. None of this changes a rule. A table can come to see it slowly, or leave the lines as rumor (*The Setting*, Appendix F: Building on Euphonia, Open for Developers, The Classes).
>
> **Planted evidence is your friend.** If the Counsellor reasoned from a forgery or a disguise, the answer follows the lie, and you don't say so. Finding the lie is the next session.

features.name: Letters of Credit
features.text:
You are a factor of a house: a bank, a merchant company, or a guild, which you and the DM choose together. You gain proficiency in the Persuasion skill and with Calligrapher's Supplies; if you already have either, choose another skill or tool. In any settlement where your house has standing (the DM decides where; most towns and cities), you can deposit coin and valuables with it and draw them out again in any other settlement where it has standing, so your wealth travels as a letter instead of a wagon.

Some houses at work around 1668:

| House | Where | Known for |
|---|---|---|
| The Genoese bankers | Genoa, and the court at Madrid | Lending to the Spanish crown against its silver fleets (the *asentistas*) |
| The Bank of Amsterdam | Amsterdam (the *Wisselbank*, 1609) | The exchange bank of Europe's trade; its bank money was trusted further than coin |
| Stockholms Banco, and the Riksbank | Stockholm | Europe's first banknotes (1661); the bank failed, and the Estates founded the Riksbank in its place in 1668 |
| The goldsmith-bankers | London (Lombard Street) | Holding merchants' deposits and lending to Charles II |
| The court Jews | The German courts | Jewish financiers who supply and finance princes and their armies, under privileges a prince can revoke (the *Hoffaktoren*, court factors) |
| The sarrafs | Istanbul and the Ottoman cities | Changing, lending, and remitting money for the court and its tax-farmers |
| The Armenian merchants of New Julfa | Isfahan, and from London to Manila | A trading network run on partnership contracts and letters |
| The Gujarati financiers | Surat, and the Indian Ocean | Moving money by the *hundi*, a bill of exchange honored from Mughal India to the Persian Gulf; Virji Vora of Surat lent to the East India Companies |
| The House of the Bird | Sofala, Mutapa's great port, and the Cape | A royal treasury that learned credit from the Swahili and Gujarati merchants it hosts, and banks platinum's wealth as paper |

features.name: Assay
features.text: By handling an object for 1 minute, you learn what it's worth on the open market and whether it's counterfeit or debased. When you Observe a creature, you can learn one of the following instead of one of Observe's usual facts: the value of what it's carrying, whose coin it's spending (who pays it, or pays for it), or whether it's in debt and to whom.

features.name: Hazard Pay
features.text: When you use Exploit on a hit made by an ally, you can roll one fewer of Exploit's dice. If you do, that ally gains Temporary Hit Points equal to a roll of your computation die plus your Intelligence modifier.

features.name: Everyone Has a Price
features.text:
As an Influence action, you make an offer to an Observed creature within 60 feet of you that can hear and understand you. The DM names its price as you make the offer: 25 GP times its Challenge Rating (minimum 10 GP). It makes a Wisdom saving throw (DC 8 plus your Intelligence modifier and Proficiency Bonus). A creature fighting for pay or plunder (a mercenary, a bandit, a hired guard) makes it normally. Any other creature has Advantage on it, since it came for something other than money.

A creature that had no allies in the fight when Initiative was rolled is harder to buy, because leaving ends the fight it came for. It has Advantage on the save if it fights for pay or plunder, and it succeeds automatically otherwise.

On a failed save, it takes the deal: it stops fighting and leaves, or stands aside if it can't leave, and it does nothing against you or your allies for the next hour unless one of you harms it. While any of its allies are still fighting you, it repeats the saving throw at the end of each of its turns; on a success, the deal is off, it rejoins the fight, and you owe it nothing. If the deal holds, you owe it its price, paid within a day. A creature you don't pay remembers.

You can use this feature twice, or three times once your Proficiency Bonus is +3 or higher, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Underwrite
features.text: When you finish a Long Rest, you can underwrite one creature: yourself or an ally. You spend the house's money on it:. The first time before your next Long Rest that the underwritten creature drops to 0 Hit Points without dying outright, the policy pays: it regains Hit Points equal to a roll of your Exploit dice. The policy pays whether or not you're there.

features.name: Debts
features.text: When a creature accepts a gift, a loan, or a favor from you that is worth at least 10 GP and that it hasn't paid for, it owes you a debt until it repays you in kind. Paying a price, a wage, or a fee creates no debt. A creature can owe you only one debt at a time. You have Advantage on Charisma checks to influence a creature that owes you a debt. You can call a creature's debt in once: the creature does one reasonable thing you ask of it that doesn't risk its life, and the debt is settled. By default, reasonable means something the creature could do in a day without losing its living or its standing.

features.name: Follow the Money
features.text:
You can spend 1 hour with ledgers (or a day of inquiries) and learn one of the following:

- **An organization's money.** With its accounts, or after a day of inquiries among the merchants it deals with: who funds it, its largest debts and debtors, and where its money is going next.
- **The House's Books.** Your house keeps the books. In a settlement where your house has standing, with its ledgers or its correspondents' letters: what one creature or organization you can name has bought, sold, borrowed, lent, or been paid there in the last month, and through whom. Money that moves through your house by letter of credit or bank draft can't move unseen, whoever sends it: a bribe, a ransom, or a spymaster's coin.

features.name: The Market
features.text: Over a week spent in a settlement where your house has standing, you can move its credit against one person or organization there: its loans are called in, its suppliers raise their prices, its hirelings hear they won't be paid. By default it costs them one holding or one hireling's loyalty, and a bigger move can cost them more: lost holdings, deserting hirelings, or a rival who suddenly has the money to act. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a week of downtime.

features.name: Card Sharp
features.text:
You gain proficiency with one Gaming Set and in the Sleight of Hand skill; if you already have either, choose another tool or skill. When you play a game with a Gaming Set you're proficient with, you can use your Intelligence modifier for any check the game calls for, and you have Advantage on checks to cheat at it and to spot someone else cheating.

Any of these can be your Gaming Set.

features.name: Where the Action Is
features.text: In any settlement, you can find where the serious play is within an hour: where it's played, who keeps the bank, and who's welcome. You can learn any game of chance or skill by watching it for 10 minutes, and in downtime you can cover your own food and lodging from the tables without spending coin.

features.name: Honest Assessment
features.text: You can use Deduction on a plan, after hearing it laid out or after watching its key people (whoever leads it and whoever carries out its essential parts; the DM tells you who they are, and you must have Observed each of them), to ask how it will go. The DM tells you whether it's likely, even, or unlikely to succeed, and the single biggest risk to it. When your assessment, given to a patron, proves right, you gain standing with that patron: you have Advantage on Charisma checks to influence it until an assessment you give it proves wrong.

features.name: The Count
features.text: Once per round, when a creature is about to make an attack roll against an Observed creature and you could use Exploit, you can call the attack before the roll (no action required). If the attack hits, you use Exploit on it and roll one more of its dice. If it misses, you can't use Exploit until the start of your next turn.

features.name: Big Player
features.text: As a Bonus Action, you signal one ally within 60 feet of yourself who can see you. It can take a Reaction to move up to its Speed, and this movement doesn't provoke Opportunity Attacks from Observed creatures. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Short or Long Rest.

features.name: Know the Odds
features.text: When you Observe a creature, you also learn its Armor Class and its current Hit Points. Tell the table as much as your character would. (For the DM: from this level, the party will know what a creature has left.)

features.name: Everyone's a Mark
features.text: When you spend an evening at play with a creature, you learn how it bets: whether it bluffs, how much it can afford to lose, and its tell. For the next week, you have Advantage on Wisdom (Insight) checks against it.

features.name: Stacked Deck
features.text: The first call you make with The Count in each combat is safe: if it misses, you can still use Exploit before the start of your next turn.

features.name: Your Own Chair
features.text: Choose one gaming house, salon, or court where the high play is. You're a fixture there: you're always admitted, and you can sit down to play on your word. When you ask, its keeper tells you who has been losing, to whom, and how much. Anyone powerful who plays there can find you for a quiet word, and you can find them. If you choose a new chair, the old one forgets you after a week.

features.name: All In
features.text: When you call an attack with The Count, you can go all in. If the attack hits, roll the attack's own damage dice twice and add both rolls together: the weapon's or the spell's dice, and no extra dice from features such as Exploit, Sneak Attack, smites, or *Hunter's Mark*. The hit doesn't count as a Critical Hit, so nothing that triggers on a Critical Hit applies; if the attack is a Critical Hit anyway, going all in adds nothing to it. If it misses, you can't use Exploit until the end of your next turn, and Stacked Deck doesn't save the call. You can go all in a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Debt of Honor
features.text: When a creature stakes something other than coin against you at play (a favor, a secret, a ship, a title) and loses, it pays, or everyone at that table knows it didn't. By default, reneging costs it its credit at that table and with everyone who heard.

subclasses.name: Hollowed
subclasses.lead: A Hollowed is a Counsellor whose computing has crowded out feeling. The mind observes, remembers, and concludes as well as any Counsellor's, and very little in it objects to what it concludes. In play, this is the Counsellor's poisoner and interrogator.

features.name: Poisoner
features.text: You gain proficiency with the Poisoner's Kit; if you already have it, choose another tool. When you finish a Long Rest, you can make doses of your poison, using your Poisoner's Kit but no other materials, until you have a number of doses equal to your Proficiency Bonus; you can't have more than that at once. A dose lasts until you finish your next Long Rest, and only you can apply it. When you use Exploit on a hit you make with a weapon, you can spend a dose (no action required). The target makes a Constitution saving throw (DC 8 plus your Intelligence modifier and Proficiency Bonus). On a failed save, it has the Poisoned condition until the end of your next turn. The extra damage from that Exploit can be Poison damage.

features.name: The Quiet Trade
features.text: You can pass as an apothecary, a physician's assistant, or a household taster without a check, and you know the poison trade wherever you go: in a settlement, a day of inquiries tells you who sells poisons, what they charge, and who has been buying.

features.name: The Wound
features.text: When you use Exploit and the target can hear and understand you, the extra damage can be Psychic damage instead: you tell it what it can't bear to hear.

features.name: Blank Stare
features.text: Wisdom (Insight) checks to read you have Disadvantage, and you have Advantage on saving throws against the Frightened condition. In addition, you can use your Intelligence modifier instead of your Charisma modifier for Charisma (Intimidation) checks, and a creature that is your prisoner, or that has the Restrained condition from you or your allies, has Disadvantage on Charisma (Deception) checks against you.

features.name: Mithridate
features.text: You have Resistance to Poison damage and Immunity to the Poisoned condition, and you can identify any poison by smell or taste without harm.

features.name: Vivisection
features.text: As an action, you can take an Observed creature apart out loud. Choose an Observed creature within 30 feet of you that can hear and understand you. It makes a Wisdom saving throw (DC 8 plus your Intelligence modifier and Proficiency Bonus). On a failed save, it takes Psychic damage equal to a roll of your computation dice, rolling a number of them equal to half your Proficiency Bonus (round up), and it can't take Reactions until the start of its next turn. Nothing happens on a successful save, but the use is still expended. This isn't magic. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Short or Long Rest.

features.name: Cause of Death
features.text: By examining a body for 10 minutes, you learn how the creature died and roughly when, and, if poison played a part, which poison and how it was given. You also learn whether a physician would have called the death natural.

features.name: Toxicology
features.text: Poison damage you deal ignores Resistance to Poison damage. A creature that has the Poisoned condition from your poison can't regain Hit Points.

features.name: Clinical
features.text: A creature that fails its saving throw against your Vivisection also has Disadvantage on the next saving throw it makes before the end of your next turn.

features.name: Taster
features.text: By handling food, drink, a letter, a glove, a ring, or a similar object for 1 minute, you know whether it's poisoned or trapped (a needle, a powder, a coated seal), and with what.

features.name: The Hollow Kill
features.text: When you use Exploit on your own attack against a Bloodied creature, roll each of Exploit's dice twice and use either roll.

features.name: Unmade
features.text: When you reduce a creature to 0 Hit Points, you can choose one creature within 30 feet of you that saw it happen. It makes a Wisdom saving throw (DC 8 plus your Intelligence modifier and Proficiency Bonus). On a failed save, it has the Frightened condition until the end of its next turn.

features.name: Underworld
features.text:
You gain proficiency with Thieves' Tools and in one of the following skills of your choice: Deception, Sleight of Hand, or Stealth. If you already have proficiency with Thieves' Tools, choose another tool. You also know Thieves' Cant.

In any settlement that has an underworld (the DM decides; every port and city does, and most towns), you can spend 1 hour asking around to find it. When you do, you find:

- *A Fence.* Someone who buys goods that can't be sold openly (stolen, smuggled, or too well known to sell) for half their value, as any merchant buys used goods, and asks nothing. By default, anything a crown or a great house is openly hunting for is too hot for any fence to touch.
- *A Market.* Someone who sells what the law there forbids or taxes: poisons, forged papers, untaxed goods, passage on a boat that leaves at night. Prices run up to double the usual; by default, half again the usual, and double for anything a crown keeps for itself.
- *A Hole.* A place to sleep where the watch doesn't come, for a few SP a night. While you and your companions lie low there, anyone searching for you in that settlement has Disadvantage on ability checks to find you.
- *The Lay of It.* Who runs the underworld there, whom it pays, and which officials it has bought.

**Your Family.** You belong to an underworld organization, a family, which you and the DM choose together: a crew, a brotherhood, a gang, a smuggling ring, or one that works in one of the underworlds in the table below. Keeping a Counsellor is a sizable expense, and every family that can afford one tries to have its own. Where your family operates, you find the underworld in 10 minutes, its Hole costs you nothing, its Market sells to you at the usual price instead of up to double, and its people do you small favors without being asked. The family's enemies are yours, though, and so are its debts.

*Neutral.* Instead of a family, you can be a freelancer: a Counsellor so well known, and so careful, that every family will use you and none will touch you. You have no home ground, but no family counts you as its enemy. You keep that only as long as you stay truly neutral: if you're seen to take a side against a family, every underworld you've worked hears of it within a week, and you have a family's enemies without a family.

Some underworlds at work around 1668:

| Underworld | Where | Known for |
|---|---|---|
| Alsatia | London: Whitefriars, and the Mint in Southwark | Old liberties where the bailiffs couldn't follow; debtors, coiners, and thieves lived there openly |
| The Cour des Miracles | Paris | Beggars' quarters where, it was said, the blind saw and the lame walked once night fell; La Reynie, Paris's first lieutenant of police (1667), was clearing them in 1668 |
| The brotherhoods of Seville | Seville, and the docks of the silver fleet | Thieves organized like a guild, with dues, ranks, a patron saint, and their own cant, *germanía* (Cervantes drew one, Monipodio's, in 1613) |
| The owlers | Romney Marsh and the English coast | Running wool to France by night, against the ban on its export (1660) |
| The gaming houses of Naples | Naples | Taking a cut of every game in the city; the word *camorra* is first recorded for them, in 1735 |
| The trades of the *ortas*, the Janissary regiments | Istanbul and the Ottoman cities | Janissaries gone into trade, running protection, smuggling, and coffeehouses under the corps' shelter |
| The sea-ban runners | Fujian, Taiwan, and the China coast | Trading past the Qing's coastal evacuation (1661), much of it for the Zheng on Taiwan, whom the Qing called pirates |
| The yakko | Edo | Rival gangs of townsmen (*machi-yakko*) and of the shogun's own bannermen (*hatamoto-yakko*); the townsmen's champion, Banzuiin Chōbei, was murdered by a bannerman in 1657 |
| Sailing without a *cartaz* | Surat, Calicut, the Gulf, Malacca | To Portugal, any Asian ship without its pass was a smuggler; to everyone else, it was a merchant |
| The *contrabandistas* | Buenos Aires and the Río de la Plata | Potosí's silver run out the back door of Spain's empire, past the fleets that were supposed to carry all of it |
| Port Royal and Curaçao | Jamaica, and the Dutch islands | Buccaneers selling Spanish prizes (Morgan sacked Portobelo in 1668), and Dutch traders running goods into Spain's colonies against its law |
| The platinum runners | Sofala, and the roads from Mutapa's mines | Carrying the king's monopoly metal past his tollkeepers, to buyers who ask nothing |

features.name: About That
features.text:
You've already thought of that. When you're in a situation you could have prepared for, you can reveal a preparation you made earlier (no action required). You must have been able to make it: you were somewhere you could have made it, with the time and the money it took. Choose one:

- *Stashed.* An item from the Adventuring Gear table, a tool, or a weapon you're proficient with, worth no more than 25 GP times your Proficiency Bonus, is on you, or hidden within 100 feet if it's too big to carry unseen. You pay its price now.
- *Greased.* One creature that would take a bribe (a guard, a porter, a clerk: by default, whoever keeps the door you need) took yours. It looks away once, leaves one door unbarred, or carries one message, and does nothing else for you. You pay its price now; the DM sets it (a few GP for a guard or a servant, much more for an official).
- *Rigged.* A door, window, gate, or lock you could have reached earlier is unlocked, or a rope, a ladder, a horse, or a boat is waiting where you need it.

The DM can rule that a preparation couldn't have been made; if so, nothing happens and the use isn't expended. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of once), and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Street Fighting
features.text:
You don't fight fair. When you use Exploit, you can roll one fewer of its dice to play one of the following tricks on the creature the attack hit:

- *Sand.* Sand in its eyes, a kick to the knee, its own cloak over its head. It has Disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the end of its next turn.
- *Lift.* If the creature is within 5 feet of you, you take one object it's carrying that weighs no more than 1 pound and that it isn't holding (a purse, a key, a letter, a vial from its belt).

features.name: Crew
features.text: In a settlement where you have found the underworld, you can hire a crew: a number of hands up to your Proficiency Bonus, at 2 GP a day each. A crew member will steal, carry, watch a door, follow someone, pick a pocket, run a message, start a brawl, or lie for you. It won't fight for you unless it's cornered, and it won't walk into danger it can see. When you set your crew a job, the crew makes one ability check for the whole job, with a bonus equal to your Proficiency Bonus plus 2. The check is the crew's: features that change your own checks don't apply to it, and anything that helps or hinders the hands doing the work does. The DM sets the DC and says what success and failure look like. A job a companion could do is offered to the companion first; the crew backs the party up and doesn't stand in for it. A crew member who's caught keeps your name out of it, unless magic gets it out. Your crew stays with you until you leave the settlement or let them go.

features.name: Play Them Off
features.text: You know a settlement's gangs, crews, and factions, what each wants, and who hates whom. Once a week, with a few days and a little money, you can set two of them against each other (a rumor, a debt sold to the wrong person, a slight in the right ear): for the next week they're busy with each other and leave you alone. By default it costs them a favor or a purse each, and the quarrel outlasts the week.

features.name: Racket
features.text: When you play a Street Fighting trick on a creature that has hit you or an ally since the end of your last turn, you don't roll one fewer die.

features.name: The Hum
features.text: Nothing moves through an underworld without you hearing of it. In a settlement where you have found the underworld, you can spend 1 hour and a few coins asking around, and then learn one of the following, if anyone in the underworld there knows it: who committed a crime in the settlement in the last month (a theft, a killing, a forgery, a smuggling run); where a stolen or smuggled thing went, and through whose hands; who in the settlement is paying for a crime to be done, and what they're paying; or what is coming into the settlement in the next week that isn't on the customs books. If the underworld doesn't know, you learn that, which is an answer of its own: whoever did it wasn't one of them.

features.name: Need to Know
features.text: You arrange the family's affairs so that each member knows only its part. When you brief a creature on a job (it must be willing, and the briefing takes 10 minutes), you decide exactly what it knows about the job, the family, and you. If magic reads its mind, compels it to tell the truth, or questions it after death, the magic learns only what you told it, and the first time that happens before your next Long Rest, you know it happened, wherever you are. You know only that it happened: not what was asked, and not by whom.

features.name: Fall Guy
features.text: Someone else always takes the fall. When Anticipate turns a hit into a miss, you can make the blow land on someone else: one creature of your choice other than the attacker or the target, within the attacker's reach (or within 5 feet of the target, for a ranged attack), takes the attack's damage as if the attack had hit it. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: The Sit-Down
features.text:
Your name is known in every underworld, and bosses ask your advice. When you find a settlement's underworld, whoever runs it receives you as an equal, and over a week spent there you can put it to work: it carries out one job you set it (a theft, a smuggling run, a jailbreak, a forgery, a riot, a fire), and you pay what the DM says the job costs. By default the job is done, and nobody can trace it to you unless it fails. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a week of downtime.

In addition, no jail or prison in a settlement where you have found the underworld holds you or your companions for more than 1d4 days, unless magic holds you there.

You can also call a sit-down: the heads of two or more of a settlement's underworld organizations meet under your guarantee, and while they sit at your table, no one there starts a fight. You have Advantage on any check to make them agree to terms.

> **Playing a Majordomo**
>
> You're not playing a villain unless you want to. The underworld is an institution like any other in 1668: it's where you go when the law is the problem, and in a world of monopolies, sea bans, and witch-finders, the law often is. The Criminal background suits you, and so does any other; plenty of majordomos were born to a counting house or trained for the law, and found the books more interesting from the other side.
>
> About That is the fun of the heist without the hour of planning at the table. Don't plan everything out loud: get into trouble, then reveal that you'd already greased the guard. Your DM is the judge of whether you could have, so be generous with each other.
>
> In a fight, you watch whoever is hurting your people, and the family's tricks ride on your friends' blows: sand in an eye, a knee kicked out, a purse gone from a belt. From 6th, a trick on whoever just hit one of yours costs you nothing. From 14th, stand where the enemies are crowded together, and let them hit each other.
>
> A family's war, a heist campaign, a smuggling ship, or a party with one Counsellor who knows a man: all of them work. By default, the family's crimes are against crowns and monopolies, and the table can set the line darker or lighter. You keep the peace between the family and the party, and you're mostly right about what each of them can live with.

features.name: Staff Officer
features.text: By watching a camp, a garrison, a fleet in harbor, or a column on the march for 10 minutes, you can estimate its numbers to within a tenth, how many days of food, water, and powder it carries, whether it has been paid lately, and whether it's getting ready to move. In any camp or garrison that isn't Hostile to you, you can find a meal, a bed, fodder for your mounts, and the officer who signs things.

features.name: Battle Picture
features.text: When you roll Initiative, you and each ally within 30 feet of you who can see or hear you can't have Disadvantage on the roll. In addition, you know the location of each Observed creature within 60 feet of you, even if it is Invisible or behind Total Cover, and an Observed creature can't hide from you.

features.name: Spotter
features.text: When you use Direct, the ally can have Advantage on the attack roll or ability check instead of adding your computation die; it decides before it rolls.

features.name: Called It
features.text: At the start of your turn, you can name an Observed creature you can see and call out loud the creature it will attack next. If the first attack roll the Observed creature makes before the start of your next turn targets the creature you called, it has Disadvantage on that roll; the warning came in time. If its first attack roll targets anyone else, the next attack roll made against it before the start of your next turn has Advantage; you read the opening it left.

features.name: Lay of the Land
features.text: You can spend 10 minutes surveying the ground from a place where you can see it. The DM tells you the best approach to any one place within 1 mile, the most defensible ground in that area, and where an ambush is most likely to be laid on the way.

features.name: Logistics
features.text: Before a journey, you can spend 1 hour with maps, stores, and anyone who knows the road. For that journey, the party's food and water last half again as long, the DM tells you where along the route more can be had and what it will cost, and you know the day the party will run out. In addition, once during that journey, when the party would be caught short, lost, or surprised on the road, you planned for it: the DM tells you so, and the party has Advantage on the first ability check or Initiative roll it causes.

features.name: Faster Than Thought
features.text: When you take a Bonus Action to Observe, you can Observe a second time as part of the same Bonus Action, choosing the same creature or another one.

features.name: Siegecraft
features.text: By studying a fortification, a walled town, or a fortified camp for 10 minutes from where you can see it, you learn its garrison's approximate strength, how long its stores will hold, its weakest point, and how a besieger would most likely take it. If you're inside the walls, you learn the same from the inside, and how long it can hold.

features.name: Fire Control
features.text: You call targets as you see them. An ally within 60 feet of you who can hear you ignores Half Cover and Three-Quarters Cover on attack rolls against Observed creatures, and doesn't have Disadvantage on attack rolls against an Observed creature for being unable to see it.

features.name: Extraction
features.text: When an ally you can see within 60 feet of you who can hear you takes damage that would reduce it to 0 Hit Points, you can take a Reaction to shout the warning; it drops to 1 Hit Point instead. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a Short or Long Rest.

features.name: Terms
features.text:
Commanders deal with you as one of their own. When you parley under a flag of truce or negotiate a surrender, a ransom, an exchange of prisoners, or passage through someone's land, you have Advantage on the Charisma checks you make, and you can use your Intelligence modifier instead of your Charisma modifier for them. A commander who has met you across a field honors a truce you've agreed to, unless it has a very good reason not to.

> **Playing a Marshal**
>
> Your turn starts with a call. Called It names whom the enemy goes for next, and an Observe on the thing that matters hands an ally your computation die (from 6th, Advantage instead). Stand where you can see the field and be heard across it: your features reach 30 to 60 feet, and you do your best work with the line between you and the enemy.
>
> On the road you earn your place every day. Logistics stretches the food and knows where more can be had, Staff Officer finds a bed in any camp that will have you, and Lay of the Land picks the ground before anyone has to fight on it.

features.name: Network
features.text:
You have someone, everywhere. When you are in a settlement, you can declare that you already have an asset inside any one place in it, however closed to you: a scullery maid in the palace, a fence in the thieves' den, a clerk in the guild hall, a novice in the temple. You can have one asset in each settlement. You have a number of **favors** equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of 1), and you regain all expended favors when you finish a Long Rest. You can spend a favor to ask an asset one question about the place where it works (who came through last night, which door the guards leave unlocked, what the abbot keeps in the strongbox). The DM answers as the asset would, which is usually, but not always, true; when it lies, the lie is the asset's own, with a reason behind it (it was paid, it was scared, it was turned). The asset won't fight, steal, or risk its life for you.

*Burned.* An asset stays yours until it is burned: exposed, gone, or turned by someone else. By default, it's burned when you call on it in a way that would expose it: a question only it could answer, acted on in front of the people it works among. The DM tells you when an asset is burned. You can't call on a burned asset again. After you finish a Long Rest, you can declare a new asset in that settlement, in the same place or another.

features.name: Human Behavior
features.text: When you Observe a creature that can speak, you can learn one of the following instead of one of Observe's usual facts: whom it answers to, what it values most, whether it is hiding something right now (not what), what it is most afraid of losing, or its price: what it would take to buy its cooperation for a day (some creatures have none, and the DM tells you so). This is an exception to Observe's rule against feelings: you read what a creature values and fears from how it lives (dress, posture, habit, the company it keeps), never from what it is thinking. For a creature with no name, the answer is the obvious one for its station; the DM needn't invent a secret for every guard.

features.name: Forewarned
features.text: When an Observed creature you can see uses an ability or casts a spell that forces a saving throw, you can take a Reaction to shout the warning. Each ally within 30 feet of you who can hear you has Advantage on its saving throw against it. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Dossiers
features.text:
You gain proficiency with the Disguise Kit and the Forgery Kit; if you already have either, choose another tool. You can Observe a creature you can hear but can't see. You can also spend 1 minute examining something a creature left behind (its handwriting, its tracks, the room it slept in) to learn facts about it as if you had Observed it (it doesn't become Observed).

*Disguise Kit.* You can use a Disguise Kit to make yourself up as a creature you have Observed, if it is roughly your size and shape. When you make a Charisma (Deception) check to pass as that creature, you can add your Intelligence modifier to the check. A creature that hasn't studied it closely and doesn't know it personally has Disadvantage on checks to see through you.

*Forgery Kit.* You can use a Forgery Kit to forge a document in the hand, voice, and seal of a creature you have Observed. You make the check with Intelligence instead of Dexterity, and with Advantage. A creature examining the forgery can make an Intelligence (Investigation) check to spot it, against a DC equal to the total of your check. It has Disadvantage on that check unless it has studied the creature you forged closely or knows it personally.

features.name: Profile
features.text:
You learn what a creature can do before it does it. When you Observe a creature, you can learn one of the following instead of one of Observe's usual facts: its most dangerous attack or ability and whether it has used it yet; how many uses it has left of something it has used (Legendary Resistance included); whether it is giving the orders to the creatures with it; whether it has allies or reinforcements nearby that you can't see; or whether it is not what it seems (disguised, shapechanged, or under another creature's control).

*Not what it seems.* In a fight, you learn this fact at a glance: a body under strain shows its seams. Outside one, it takes the minute of study Dossiers describes (watching the creature, or examining what it left behind), and you learn *that* something is wrong and what kind of wrong (the walk, the hand, the eyes), not who or what is underneath.

features.name: Read the Room
features.text: When you enter a space where creatures are gathered (a hall, a camp, a tavern), you can Observe a number of creatures you can see equal to your Proficiency Bonus (no action required), learning Observe's facts about only one of them, your choice. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a Short or Long Rest. In addition, an Observed creature can't have Advantage on attack rolls against you.

features.name: Without Portfolio
features.text: You answer to no one who can be named. When an official in a settlement where you have declared an asset orders you or an ally detained, searched, or arrested, orders your property seized, or bars your way, you can spend a favor to make that order go astray: the paperwork is lost, a superior countermands it, or someone else is taken in your place. The order can't be given again against you or that ally until the next dawn. This has no effect on anyone acting outside the law, and the settlement's ruler, or anyone who has studied you closely, can push the order through.

features.name: The Club
features.text:
You can run your Network without leaving your chair. The Club (*The Setting*, Powers and Factions, The Crowns and the Churches, The Spymaster's Club) keeps a few pairs of shewstones, the rarest of things (Sending Stones, in the rules), and you have the use of them. When you spend a favor, you can call on an asset in any settlement where you have ever declared one, anywhere in the world: the message goes by shewstone to the Club's agent there, and the answer reaches you within 1 day.

> **The Spymaster's facts, in one place**
>
> When you Observe, you choose from these:
>
> - *Every Counsellor:* its highest ability score; its weakest saving throw; a Resistance, Immunity, or Vulnerability; whether it's Bloodied; whether it's hurt, sick, exhausted, drunk, or poisoned; its trade or station; whether it's armed or carrying something concealed.
> - *Human Behavior (3rd), a creature that can speak:* whom it answers to; what it values most; whether it's hiding something right now; what it's most afraid of losing; its price.
> - *Profile (6th):* its most dangerous attack or ability, and whether it has used it; uses left of something it has used; whether it gives the orders; unseen allies or reinforcements nearby; whether it's not what it seems (outside a fight, a minute's study).

multiclass.text: You must have an Intelligence score of 13 or higher. Gain the following trait from the Core Counsellor Traits table: Hit Point Die. Gain the Counsellor's level 1 features, which are listed in the Counsellor Features table. If you have more levels in another class than in this one, Exploit, Sidestep, and Anticipate share one pool of uses in place of their own limits. The pool holds twice your Counsellor level, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest (not a Short Rest). Wider Gaze doesn't remove this limit, and Exploit still works only once between the starts of your turns.

data.name: Courtier
data.blurb: A new class. The accomplished person of every court's ideal, who makes it all look effortless.

traits.value: Simple weapons, and Martial weapons that have the Finesse property
*Choose 1:* one type of Artisan's Tools, Calligrapher's Supplies, Disguise Kit, or a Gaming Set
*Choose A or B:* (A) Rapier, Dagger, Shortbow, 20 Arrows, Quiver, Fine Clothes, Diplomat's Pack, the tool you chose, and 10 GP; or (B) 120 GP.

rows.Class Features: Accomplishments and Regard, Ease, Effortless Arms, Learned Magic
Expertise, Ease in a Fight, Weapon Mastery

features.name: Accomplishments and Regard
features.text:
You have made yourself accomplished. You gain two accomplishments from the list below, and you gain more as you reach Courtier levels, as shown in the Accomplishments column of the Courtier Features table. Each accomplishment is one choice. The arts in parentheses after its name (Arms, Letters, Muses, Society, or Mysteries) are what it can count as for your Regard: when an accomplishment lists two, choose one when you take it, and it counts as that art for as long as you have it. The accomplishments are listed by the level you need to take them. Unless an accomplishment says otherwise, you can't choose the same one twice. Whenever you gain a Courtier level, you can replace one accomplishment with another for which you qualify.

**The forgone art.** At level 3 you join a college, and four of the five colleges forgo one art: the College of Arms forgoes Letters, the College of Art forgoes Mysteries, the College of Psyche forgoes Muses, and the College of Verse forgoes Arms. The College of Grace forgoes none, and no college forgoes Society, since every courtier lives in it. This is the whole rule:

- None of your accomplishments can count as the forgone art, so your Regard can be at most 4 (5 for Grace).
- You can't take an accomplishment that lists only the forgone art. One that lists two arts counts as the other.
- When you join the college, each accomplishment you have that counts as the forgone art switches to its other art. If it lists no other, replace it with an accomplishment you qualify for.
- Forgoing an art changes your accomplishments and your Regard, and nothing else. You keep your weapons, your spells, and every class feature, and your college's features work even if they draw on the art it forgoes.

If you know your college at level 1, leave its forgone art out of your choices, and nothing changes at level 3.

**Regard.** You have presence, and you see everyone else's. Your **Regard** is the number of different arts (Arms, Letters, Muses, Society, and Mysteries) among your accomplishments. Several of your features grow with your Regard; each says how.

**The Read.** When you can see and hear a group of creatures for 1 minute, or as a Study action in combat, you learn the following about a number of them up to your Regard: each one's attitude toward you; which of them has the most authority over the others, and which has the most actual power; and whether any of them is hiding hostility toward you or your companions.

**Never a Misstep.** You never commit a breach of manners by accident. In any court, house, or company, you know the forms of precedence, address, and courtesy as if you'd been raised among them, even if you've never seen their like before. You have Advantage on Charisma checks to be accepted as belonging somewhere you don't.

> **For the DM.** The Read is a reveal, and it comes whenever the Courtier asks. For any room a Courtier walks into, decide who really holds power there, and keep a line on each important creature's attitude. A Read shows *that* a creature is hiding hostility, never why, or what it means to do about it.

**From Courtier level 1**

***A Secret (Mysteries).*** Choose one spell from the Courtier spell list, of a level for which you have spell slots. You always have it prepared. It counts as a Courtier spell for you and doesn't count against your number of prepared spells, and once per Long Rest you can cast it without expending a spell slot. You can take this accomplishment twice, choosing a different spell each time.

***An Instrument of Your Art (Muses).*** You gain proficiency with one musical instrument, one type of Artisan's Tools, or the Disguise Kit, and you have Advantage on ability checks you make with it. A work you make with it, given as a gift, earns you an audience with the person who receives it. You can take this accomplishment more than once, choosing a different tool each time.

***Correspondence (Letters, Society).*** You gain proficiency with Calligrapher's Supplies and the Forgery Kit. A letter you write in your own hand is opened and read by its recipient before any other mail, whoever they are, and you can tell when a letter you receive has been opened and resealed on the way, whether by a postmaster or a *cabinet noir*.

***Every Table (Society, Muses).*** You gain proficiency in two of these skills: Deception, Insight, Intimidation, or Persuasion.

***Fencing Style (Arms).*** You gain a Fighting Style feat of your choice. You can take this accomplishment twice, choosing a different feat each time.

***Horse and Bow (Arms).*** You gain proficiency with Longbows and in the Animal Handling skill, and you have Advantage on checks and saving throws to stay mounted.

***Patronage (Society, Muses).*** You have a patron at one court or great house of your choice (a king's chamber, a cardinal's household, a factor of Mutapa's House of the Bird) who will receive you, lend you modest sums, and speak for you to that court's authorities. If you lose the patron, you can find another at a different court after a month there.

***The Code (Arms, Society).*** You know the customs of the duel in any land you've lived in: who can challenge whom, over what, with which weapons, and what the law will overlook. You can serve as a second, and a challenge you carry or accept is honored by both sides. Before a fight that begins with words, you can tell whether the other side means to keep the forms.

***The Gaming House (Society, Letters).*** You gain proficiency with two Gaming Sets, and you always know when a game you're watching is crooked.

***The Hunt (Arms, Society).*** You gain proficiency in the Survival skill, and you keep a trained hawk or a brace of hounds that hunts for you but never fights. You're welcome at any hunt a court holds, and whoever rides beside you there speaks more freely than they would indoors.

***The Library (Letters).*** You gain proficiency in two of these skills: Arcana, History, Nature, or Religion.

***The Second Weapon (Arms).*** You gain proficiency with one Martial weapon of your choice, and you can use the mastery property of one kind of weapon you're proficient with (one more kind once you have Weapon Mastery).

***The Stage (Muses).*** You gain proficiency in the Performance skill and with the Disguise Kit. When you perform for at least 1 minute, you can choose one creature in the audience: if it isn't Hostile, its attitude toward you improves by one step until your next Long Rest, unless you give it reason otherwise.

***Tongues (Letters, Society).*** You learn two languages of your choice, and you can read any script used to write a language you know, however archaic. You can take this accomplishment more than once.

**From Courtier level 11**

From level 11, any accomplishment you gain or swap in can be one of these; your seventh comes at level 11.

***A Crown's Commission (Muses, Society).*** You hold an appointment as artist to one sovereign of your choice. While you serve, you have lodging at that court, a pension of 50 GP a month, and a place in its ceremonies, and your work hangs where everyone who matters will see it. Once per month you can ask the sovereign's household a favor that costs it nothing but attention: an introduction, a pass through a closed gate, a seat at a dinner.

***A Great Work (Mysteries, Muses).*** Choose one level 6 spell from any class's spell list, of any school: the great work is the one time a courtier reaches past their own kind of magic. You always have it prepared, it counts as a Courtier spell for you, and you can cast it once without expending a spell slot; you regain that use when you finish a Long Rest. It stays one spell as it grows: when you reach Courtier levels 13, 15, and 17, you can replace it with one a level higher (level 7, then 8, then 9), and your level 9 Great Work can be *Wish* (with all of that spell's usual risks).

> **For the DM.** A Great Work is one spell, cast once per Long Rest, and the Courtier has no other spell above level 5. Run a Courtier's *Wish* as you would any caster's: copying another spell is safe, and anything bigger carries the spell's own stress.

***A Master's Salle (Arms, Society).*** You keep a fencing school in a city of your choice, and its pupils, from the younger children of great houses to princes, owe you a student's loyalty. In that city, or at any court where one of them now serves (the DM says who's there; usually at least one pupil), you can call on a pupil once a month for a sword at your side, a message carried, or a word in the right ear. A challenge issued in your school's name is always answered, and always by the person challenged.

***The Ear of the King (Society, Arms).*** Once per month, you can have a private audience of a few minutes with any ruler who has received you before, without going through their ministers. What you say reaches them exactly as you say it. What they do about it is theirs.

***The Republic of Letters (Letters, Mysteries).*** You keep a correspondence with scholars in the great cities of the world, from the Royal Society to the madrasas of Isfahan. Any library, archive, academy, or college admits you as a colleague. Once a week, a letter to your correspondents brings back an answer to one question of learning (history, law, languages, natural philosophy, or theology) as accurate as the learned world can make it, in the time the post takes.

features.name: Ease
features.text:
You make the hardest things look effortless, and sometimes that makes them so. You have a number of Ease points shown in the Ease column of the Courtier Features table. You regain all expended Ease when you finish a Short or Long Rest. You can spend Ease on the following options, each costing 1 Ease.

- **Make It Look Easy.** When you fail an ability check, you can spend 1 Ease to add your Charisma modifier (minimum of +1) to the roll, possibly turning it into a success.
- **With Ease.** Before you make a Charisma check, you can spend 1 Ease to treat the d20 roll as 10 plus your Regard.
- **First Through the Door.** When you roll Initiative, you can spend 1 Ease to add your Charisma modifier to the roll. If you do, you can move up to half your Speed immediately, without provoking Opportunity Attacks.
- **Not a Hair Out of Place.** When a creature you can see hits you with an attack roll while you aren't wearing Medium or Heavy armor or holding a Shield, you can take a Reaction and spend 1 Ease to add your Charisma modifier to your AC against that attack, possibly turning the hit into a miss. The DM tells you the attack's total before you decide.

You gain more options at level 2 (Ease in a Fight) and level 3 (A Light Touch, in Telling Cut).

features.name: Effortless Arms
features.text: When you make an attack roll with a weapon that has the Finesse property, you can use your Charisma modifier instead of your Strength or Dexterity modifier for the attack and damage rolls.

features.name: Learned Magic
features.text:
You have learned a little magic from every tradition that would teach you. The Courtier spell list, after this class's features, gathers it: spells of presence, the mask, the read, and the ward, from every class's list.

**Cantrips.** You know *Prestidigitation*, *Mending*, and *Message* (the small magic of a person who is always presentable, whose lace is never torn, and who can say a word across a crowded room), and two cantrips of your choice from the Courtier spell list. Whenever you gain a Courtier level, you can replace one of the two with another from the list.

**Prepared Spells of Level 1+.** You prepare the list of level 1+ spells that are available for you to cast with this feature. To start, choose two level 1 spells from the Courtier spell list. The number of spells on your list increases as you gain Courtier levels, as shown in the Prepared Spells column of the Courtier Features table. Whenever that number increases, choose more spells from the Courtier spell list until the number on your list matches the table. Each spell must be of a level for which you have spell slots.

**Changing Your Prepared Spells.** Whenever you gain a Courtier level, you can replace one spell on your list with another from the Courtier spell list for which you have spell slots.

**Spell Slots.** The Courtier Features table shows how many spell slots you have. You regain all expended slots when you finish a Long Rest.

**Spellcasting Ability.** Charisma is your spellcasting ability for your Courtier spells.

**Spellcasting Focus.** You can use any tool, musical instrument, or weapon you're proficient with as a Spellcasting Focus for your Courtier spells.

features.name: Expertise
features.text: You gain Expertise in two of your skill proficiencies of your choice. At Courtier level 9, you gain Expertise in two more.

features.name: Ease in a Fight
features.text:
Your ease reaches further into a fight. Make It Look Easy now works on saving throws as well as ability checks, and you gain this Ease option:

- **The Riposte.** When a creature you can see misses you with a melee attack, you can take a Reaction and spend 1 Ease to make one weapon attack against it.

You have one Reaction, so the choice is the art: hold it for Not a Hair Out of Place and the blow that would land, or spend it on the one that didn't.

features.name: Weapon Mastery
features.text: Your training with weapons allows you to use the mastery properties of two kinds of weapons of your choice with which you have proficiency, such as Rapiers and Shortbows. Whenever you finish a Long Rest, you can change the kinds of weapons you chose.

features.name: Courtier College
features.text: You gain a Courtier College of your choice: the art that finishes you. The College of Arms, the College of Art, the College of Grace, the College of Psyche, and the College of Verse are detailed after this class's description. You gain each of your college's features at the Courtier levels shown.

features.name: Telling Cut
features.text:
Once on each of your turns when you hit a creature with a weapon attack, the creature takes extra Psychic damage equal to a roll of your Telling Cut die plus your Charisma modifier, and it can't make Opportunity Attacks against you until the start of its next turn. Your Telling Cut die is shown in the Telling Cut column of the Courtier Features table.

**A Light Touch.** When your Telling Cut lands, you can also spend 1 Ease to deal 1d8 extra damage of the weapon's type. The extra damage becomes 2d8 at Courtier level 11.

features.name: Ability Score Improvement
features.text: You gain the Ability Score Improvement feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. You gain this feature again at Courtier levels 8, 12, and 16.

features.name: Extra Attack
features.text: You can attack twice instead of once whenever you take the Attack action on your turn.

features.name: Coming and Going
features.text:
As a Bonus Action, you can choose to be noticed or to be overlooked, for 10 minutes or until you choose again.

- *Noticed.* Every creature that can see you and isn't Hostile to you stops what it's doing to watch or listen to you for as long as you hold its attention: until the effect ends, or until something more pressing (taking damage, a threat, its own urgent business) calls it away. A creature with Truesight, or that is in combat, is unaffected.
- *Overlooked.* Creatures that can see you pay you no more attention than a servant, unless you attack, cast a spell, or speak to them. You have Advantage on Dexterity (Stealth) checks to go unnoticed in a crowd.

You can do this a number of times equal to your Regard, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.

features.name: Quick Study
features.text: If you watch a creature use a skill or a tool for at least 1 minute, or study a book or a teacher for an hour, you gain proficiency in that skill or with that tool until you finish a Long Rest. You can have only one proficiency from this feature at a time. You can't gain Expertise in a skill or tool you're proficient in only through this feature.

features.name: Witnessed
features.text: When two or more creatures make an agreement in your presence and you say aloud that you witness it, the agreement is witnessed. Each party knows when another breaks it. A creature that breaks a witnessed agreement has Disadvantage on Charisma checks against every party to it, and against you, until it makes amends that the injured party accepts. You can have a number of witnessed agreements at once equal to your Regard.

features.name: Unshaken
features.text: You can't gain the Charmed or Frightened condition against your will. When a creature tries to Charm or Frighten you and fails, you can spend 1 Ease to turn it back: that creature must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw against your spell save DC or have the condition it tried to give you, toward you, until the end of its next turn.

features.name: Never Without Ease
features.text: When you roll Initiative and have fewer than 2 Ease points, you regain Ease until you have 2.

features.name: Epic Boon
features.text: You gain an Epic Boon feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. Boon of Fate is recommended.

features.name: The Sun Rises
features.text:
As a Bonus Action, you can become the center of the world for 1 minute. For the duration, you regain all your Ease, and the following benefits apply:

- Your allies within 60 feet of you that can see you add your Charisma modifier to their attack rolls and saving throws.
- Hostile creatures within 60 feet of you that can see you have Disadvantage on attack rolls against any target other than you.
- Your Regard counts as 5 (6 where Grace's Reputation applies).

Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a Long Rest.

> **Playing a Courtier**
>
> You fence, you cast, and you read every room you walk into. In a fight, you're first through the door, you fence with Charisma, and every hit tells. Ease is how it all looks effortless: a failed save made good, a hit turned into a miss, a miss punished with a riposte.
>
> Try the showy thing. Make It Look Easy pays out after you fail, so the daring attempt (the leap, the bluff, the toast to the enemy's face) is the one the class covers.
>
> A courtier collects accomplishments from every art, because your Regard, and with it your presence, grows with every new art you take up. Out of a fight, you know who matters in any court on earth, and you never put a foot wrong in front of them.

subclasses.name: Arms
subclasses.lead: * The fencing schools of Madrid, Bologna, and Edo; the circle drawn on the floor of the salle; the duel at dawn and the code that governs it. Arms is stillness: one cut, placed exactly.*

features.name: The Sword or the Book
features.text:
Your college forgoes Letters. In exchange, you gain proficiency in the Athletics skill (if you already have it, choose another skill instead), and the master of any fencing school will open the salle to you and let you train there.

**Affairs of Honor.** You have The Code without spending an accomplishment on it (if you already have it, you gain one more accomplishment from the art of Arms instead), and people of rank bring you their quarrels: a duel you arrange is fought by its terms, and the magistrates hear of it last. Roll on the table below when someone comes to you for satisfaction.

features.name: The Challenge
features.text: As a Bonus Action, you can challenge one creature you can see within 30 feet of you. The Challenge lasts for 1 minute, and it ends early if you attack a different creature on your turn, or if you challenge someone else. The code binds both sides: while the Challenge lasts, you can use The Riposte against the challenged creature whenever it makes an attack roll against a creature other than you, as well as when it misses you. Once you reach Courtier level 5, you also have Advantage on the first attack roll you make against the creature you've challenged on each of your turns.

features.name: The Circle
features.text: Your Challenge draws the circle for you. While your Challenge lasts, the creature you've challenged provokes an Opportunity Attack from you when it enters your reach, and you don't provoke Opportunity Attacks from it.

features.name: Economy
features.text: When you take the Attack action and could make more than one attack, you can make one attack instead. On a hit, it deals extra damage equal to a second roll of the weapon's damage dice plus your Charisma modifier, and your next use of The Riposte before the start of your next turn costs no Ease. Every turn asks the duelist's question: two cuts, or one cut and wait.

features.name: Example
features.text: When the one cut from Economy hits the creature you've challenged, one ally who can see you can take a Reaction to make one weapon attack against a creature of its choice. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a Short or Long Rest.

features.name: One Cut
features.text: When you hit a creature with an attack, you can make the hit a Critical Hit, and the creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls and saving throws until the end of its next turn. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a Long Rest.

subclasses.name: Art
subclasses.lead: * Painting with light at its heart, with sculpture, architecture, and gardens around it: Hoogstraten's perspective boxes in Dordrecht, the Kanō painters' gold screens and sliding doors for the shogun's castles in Edo and Kyoto, and the four-part gardens of Isfahan and Agra.*

features.name: What the Eye Can See
features.text: Your college forgoes Mysteries, the study of magic for its own sake. Your magic goes into your painting, and this college's features are that magic. You keep your Courtier spells; you study no magic beyond them. In exchange, you gain proficiency with Painter's Supplies and one other type of Artisan's Tools (if you already have either, choose another tool instead).

features.name: Highlight
features.text:
As a Bonus Action, you can spend 1 Ease to paint the field with light and shadow for 1 minute. Choose one creature you can see within 60 feet of you to light and one creature you can see within 60 feet of you to shadow. On each of your later turns while the painting lasts, you can move the light, the shadow, or both to other creatures you can see within 60 feet of you as a Bonus Action.

- *Lit.* The lit creature can't benefit from the Invisible condition or from being hidden, and it sheds Dim Light in a 5-foot radius. The first attack roll made against it each round adds a roll of your Telling Cut die to the attack roll.
- *Shadowed.* The first attack roll made against the shadowed creature each round has Disadvantage, and it can take the Hide action as a Bonus Action even if it's only in Dim Light.

features.name: The Likeness
features.text:
With 1 hour of work and Painter's Supplies, you can paint a likeness of a creature you can see. While you carry it, you have Advantage on ability checks to recognize the sitter however it's disguised and on Wisdom (Insight) checks against it; you know if the sitter dies, and roughly how (the paint darkens, cracks, or runs); and the likeness counts as a likeness for spells such as *Scrying*, but no one can scry the sitter through it unless you allow it. You can carry a number of likenesses equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum of 1).

**Commissions.** Your work hangs in great houses, and a garden, a ceiling, or a portrait you made is a door into any house that owns it: its household will receive you as a guest. Roll on the commission table below when you're between jobs.

features.name: Trompe-l'oeil
features.text:
When you take the Attack action, you can replace one of your attacks with a painting: spend 1 Ease and choose one:

- *A Painted Wall.* A wall up to 15 feet long, 10 feet high, and 1 inch thick appears in unoccupied spaces within 60 feet of you until the start of your next turn. It blocks movement and line of sight, and attacks can't pass through it.
- *A Painted Door.* You paint a door on a wall, floor, or ceiling no more than 5 feet thick within 30 feet of you. Until the start of your next turn, any creature can pass through it as if it were open. A creature inside the wall when the door closes is shunted to the nearer side.
